Backward
BAK-werd
adv. & a.
From back and the Anglo-Saxon suffix -weard, denoting direction. Webster 1828: with the back in advance; toward the back; on the back part. Scripture makes the direction a moral one: to go backward is to apostatize, and the two occasions when men fall backward are both moments of holy dread.

Biblical Definition

Twice in Scripture men walk backward and it is reverence; once a nation goes backward and it is ruin. Shem and Japheth cover their father without looking: And Shem and Japheth took a garment, and laid it upon both their shoulders, and went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father; and their faces were backward, and they saw not their father's nakedness (Genesis 9:23). The awkward gait is the whole point — they take deliberate trouble not to see what Ham had gone and told. Against this stands Isaiah’s indictment, where the same direction is covenant treachery: Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity... they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward (Isaiah 1:4). Apostasy in Scripture is rarely a leap; it is a walking away with the face still pointed at the sanctuary. In the garden the arresting party discovers what happens when the divine name is spoken by the One it belongs to: As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground (John 18:6). And Hezekiah is given the strangest sign in the Old Testament: the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward (Isaiah 38:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BACKWARD as with the back in advance; toward the back; on the back part; toward past times; and figuratively, unwilling, averse, reluctant, slow.

expand to see more

BACKWARD, adv. — With the back in advance; as, to move backward.

Toward past times or events; as, to look backward on the history of man.

By way of reflection; retrospectively.

BACKWARD, a. — Unwilling; averse; reluctant; hesitating; also, slow; sluggish; dilatory.

From back and -ward, the Anglo-Saxon weard, direction, as in toward, homeward.

Key Scripture

Genesis 9:23 — "And Shem and Japheth took a garment, and laid it upon both their shoulders, and went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father; and their faces were backward, and they saw not their father's nakedness."

Isaiah 1:4 — "Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward."

John 18:6 — "As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground."

Isaiah 38:8 — "Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down."

Modern Corruption

Genesis 9:23 commends men for refusing to look, which cuts directly against the modern conviction that exposure is honesty and discretion is repression.

expand to see more

Ham saw and told; his brothers walked backward and covered. Scripture blesses the two who declined the information. This is the opposite of the reigning instinct, which treats the uncovering of a father’s shame as candour, authenticity, or overdue truth-telling, and treats the covering of it as complicity. The Bible knows the difference between the sin that must be confronted by the elders and the nakedness that must simply be covered by a son. Charity shall cover the multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8), and love beareth all things (1 Corinthians 13:7). A culture organized around public exposure — of parents, of pastors, of the dead — has mistaken Ham’s posture for virtue. The fifth commandment stands over this text, and so does the curse that followed the telling.

Isaiah 1:4 names the manner of apostasy exactly: gone away backward. Men do not usually renounce the faith; they reverse out of it slowly while still facing the right way. The Reformed doctrine of perseverance is often misheard as a promise that nothing of the sort can happen to a professing believer, but the confession is more careful. Perseverance is the genuine fruit of regeneration, not a guarantee attached to a past decision, and the same Scriptures that promise the elect shall not finally fall warn continually against drawing back. Hebrews 10:38-39 holds both together in a sentence. The bare formula once saved always saved, detached from any expectation of fruit, is not the doctrine of the 1689 Confession, and Isaiah 1 is what it looks like when a whole nation keeps the outward face and moves the feet.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew achor (H268), the hinder part, backward; nazor (H2114), to be estranged or go away backward; Greek opiso (G3694), backward, behind.

expand to see more

Hebrew achor (H268) — the hinder part; their faces were backward (Genesis 9:23), and the shadow returned backward (Isaiah 38:8).

Hebrew nazor (H2114) — to be estranged, to turn away; they are gone away backward (Isaiah 1:4).

Greek opiso (G3694) — backward, to the rear; they went backward, and fell to the ground (John 18:6).

Hebrew maalah (H4609) — a step or degree, the marks on the dial of Ahaz (Isaiah 38:8).

Hebrew ervah (H6172) — nakedness, shame; the thing covered in Genesis 9:23 and legislated in Leviticus 18.

Usage

"They went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father (Genesis 9:23) — the awkward gait is the point; they take trouble not to see."

"They are gone away backward (Isaiah 1:4) — apostasy walks away with its face still toward the sanctuary."

"I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground (John 18:6) — the arresting party meets the divine name and cannot stand."
